Gold price in EUR, GBP, AUD, CHF — live multi-currency guide

Gold is quoted globally in US dollars — but if you live in Europe, the UK, Australia, or Switzerland, the price in your currency is what actually matters for your purchasing power.

Why the gold price differs by currency

Gold has one global spot price, denominated in US dollars per troy ounce. That price is the same whether you're in New York, Frankfurt, or Sydney. But the moment you convert it to euros, pounds, or Australian dollars, the foreign exchange rate comes into play — and that rate moves independently of gold itself.

This creates an interesting dynamic: gold can be flat in USD terms but rising sharply in EUR terms if the euro is weakening against the dollar. Investors in weaker-currency countries often see gold performing better in their local currency than US investors do — which is part of why gold's appeal as a store of value is even stronger outside the US.

Gold price in major currencies (how to read it)

All major gold price websites, including GoldAlert, convert the USD spot price using real-time FX rates. The conversion is straightforward: divide the USD price by the USD/local currency exchange rate.

Example with gold at $2,800/oz:

  • Gold in EUR: $2,800 ÷ 1.09 (EUR/USD rate) = approx. €2,569/oz
  • Gold in GBP: $2,800 ÷ 1.27 (GBP/USD rate) = approx. £2,205/oz
  • Gold in AUD: $2,800 × 1.54 (USD/AUD rate) = approx. A$4,312/oz
  • Gold in CHF: $2,800 ÷ 1.12 (CHF/USD rate) = approx. CHF 2,500/oz
  • Gold in CAD: $2,800 × 1.36 (USD/CAD rate) = approx. C$3,808/oz
  • Gold in JPY: $2,800 × 149 (USD/JPY rate) = approx. ¥417,200/oz

These figures are illustrative — the actual price updates in real time and your currency's exchange rate changes continuously during market hours.

Gold in euros (XAUEUR)

The eurozone gold price (XAUEUR) is particularly significant because the European Central Bank holds large gold reserves, and European investors have historically had high gold allocation relative to equity markets. Gold in euros has trended strongly upward over the past decade as the ECB maintained low rates and the euro experienced multiple crises. Tracking XAUEUR separately from XAUUSD gives a cleaner picture of gold performance for European investors.

Gold in British pounds (XAUGBP)

UK investors tracking gold in GBP (XAUGBP) have seen amplified gains during periods of pound weakness — notably after the 2016 Brexit referendum, when sterling fell sharply and gold in pounds hit new records even though the USD gold price had not. For British buyers, measuring gold performance in GBP is more relevant than the headline USD figure.

Gold in Australian dollars (XAUAUD)

Australia is one of the world's largest gold producers. The AUD gold price (XAUAUD) is closely watched by mining companies and investors there. Because the Australian dollar often moves with commodity prices, XAUAUD can behave differently from XAUUSD — when commodities broadly rise, AUD strengthens, which can suppress the local gold price even as mining revenues rise.

Gold in Swiss francs (XAUCHF)

Switzerland is home to some of the world's largest gold refineries (PAMP, Valcambi, Argor-Heraeus). The Swiss franc is itself considered a safe-haven currency, so XAUCHF sometimes moves less dramatically than XAUUSD during crises — both the franc and gold tend to rise together in a flight to safety, partially offsetting each other in CHF terms.

How to track gold in your currency on GoldAlert

GoldAlert's Signal Board shows gold prices in multiple currencies simultaneously. Use the currency selector at the top of the page to switch between USD, EUR, GBP, AUD, CHF, CAD, and JPY.
